## Proof

A semidirect product of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ by $\mathbb{Z}_q$ is a group of order $pq$ in which $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is the normal subgroup and $\mathbb{Z}_q$ acts on it via a homomorphism
$$\varphi: \mathbb{Z}_q \to \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_p).$$

Since $p$ is prime, $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is cyclic of prime order, so
$$\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_p) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{p-1},$$
the cyclic group of order $p-1$.

The isomorphism type of the semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}_p \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}_q$ is determined (up to isomorphism) by the homomorphism $\varphi$, up to automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}_q$ and $\mathbb{Z}_p$. Let us classify the homomorphisms $\varphi$.

A homomorphism $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}_q \to \mathbb{Z}_{p-1}$ is determined by the image of a generator $g$ of $\mathbb{Z}_q$. The element $\varphi(g)$ must satisfy $\varphi(g)^q = e$, i.e., its order must divide $q$. Since $q$ is prime, the order of $\varphi(g)$ is either $1$ or $q$.

- **Order 1:** $\varphi(g) = e$, giving the trivial homomorphism. This yields the direct product $\mathbb{Z}_p \times \mathbb{Z}_q \cong \mathbb{Z}_{pq}$.

- **Order $q$:** This requires an element of order $q$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{p-1}$, which exists if and only if $q \mid (p-1)$, i.e., if and only if $(p-1)/q$ is an integer.

By hypothesis, $(p-1)/q$ is **not** an integer, so $q \nmid (p-1)$. Therefore $\mathbb{Z}_{p-1}$ contains no element of order $q$, and the only homomorphism $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}_q \to \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ is the trivial one.

Hence there is exactly **one** semidirect product, namely the direct product $\mathbb{Z}_p \times \mathbb{Z}_q \cong \mathbb{Z}_{pq}$.

$$\boxed{1}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
